messages.author: 321fe6c60966e560
messages.subject: observer variability
parts:
Dear List,

I am analyzing data from a point transect study where observer variability
is huge! Both observers were experienced, with equally good bird
identification skills, although Observer 2 was more experienced with
distance estimation than Observer 1. While species abundances were
comparable, the shapes of their distributions were very different.
Observer 1 tended to heap her detections in the first two intervals
resulting in left-skewed distributions as opposed to the humped
distributions of Observer 2. It appears that Observer 1 may have been
underestimating distances. Is there a way to adjust the distributions of
Observer 1 so that I can potentially pool both observers? For example, if
I calculate the average proportion per distance interval across species
from Observer 1, could I use these proportions to transform those data
from Observer 1? Is this a reasonable approach?

Thanks and Happy Thanksgiving!
Kim Ferree

messages.author: 870960174f1c372c
messages.subject: Re: observer variability
parts:
Kimberly,

My $0.02:

If either observer is recording incorrect measurements then any
"corrections" are a shot in the dark and not supported by your data.

If your observers actually recorded the correct distances, then differences
in their data reflect real differences in their detection processes. It seems
reasonable that a "new" distance observer, having been repeatedly told
that g(0) must be perfect, will focus her attention near the point. If this
is
the case, what is the problem with estimating two seperate detection
functions and make density estimates appropriately? Any "correction" you
make will not change the fact the Pa is different for the two observers.

My best advice is to take a close look at your assumptions (g0, movement,
accurate distances, etc.). If you believe they are met, just estimate
different detection rates for each observer (assuming the
post-stratification by observer is supported by AIC) and don't worry about
why they are different. Don't fool with some ad hoc "correction" just so you
can pool the data. It is unnecessary and unsupportable.

Good luck!

~Aaron Ellingson

> > is huge! Both observers were experienced, with equally good bird
> > identification skills, although Observer 2 was more experienced with
> > distance estimation than Observer 1. While species abundances were
> > comparable, the shapes of their distributions were very different.
> > Observer 1 tended to heap her detections in the first two intervals
> > resulting in left-skewed distributions as opposed to the humped
> > distributions of Observer 2. It appears that Observer 1 may have been
> > underestimating distances. Is there a way to adjust the distributions of
> > Observer 1 so that I can potentially pool both observers? For example, if
> > I calculate the average proportion per distance interval across species
> > from Observer 1, could I use these proportions to transform those data
> > from Observer 1? Is this a reasonable approach?

Kimberly, errors in distance estimation cause serious bias in point
transect sampling. By far the best way to resolve it is through proper
observer training, and use of laser rangefinders - which now only cost
$200 in the US - substantially more elsewhere, but you can get them
shipped from the US - e.g. from www.binoculars.com.

The advanced distance sampling book is due out next year - in it, there
will be a section on estimation when there are measurement errors, but to
do anything useful, you really need to have a subset of detections whose
distances are known. You could retrospectively have your two observers
estimate some distances to singing birds that you later determine exactly.
Of course, it is possible that the observers will behave differently now,
especially if they know that there has been a problem with their distance
estimates.

Steve Buckland
